channel.title: The Dig — Software stack: compilers and pulse level
channel.description: Papers relevant to operating, benchmarking, integrating and using a semiconductor spin-qubit quantum computer of at least 16 qubits that is co-located with and integrated into an HPC system. Today's arXiv announcement, ranked against the Software stack: compilers and pulse level preset. Today’s ranked reading list is led by 2611.30931, a must-read on calibration-insensitive spin-qubit pulses that sustain 99.97% fidelity and stable rotation angles over ten days in Si/SiGe, directly targeting drift and recalibration. The remaining skims span adjacent practical concerns: 2611.32388 offers shallow-circuit thermal-state preparation ideas transferable mainly through depth reduction; 2611.30508 and 2611.32560 provide low-resource QAOA constructions and application heuristics relevant to small noisy spin-qubit benchmarks; 2611.29983 presents a calibration-aware compilation and backend stack but lacks spin-qubit and HPC evidence; and 2611.31514 frames DOE-scale HPC-quantum integration strategy without concrete spin-qubit control or middleware methods. No pay dirt today — 2 to skim.

item.title: Thermal state preparation with shallow quantum circuits
item.description:
Skim new method — PP-VarQITE produces state-preparation circuits that are two to ten times shallower than sequential MPS compilations across frustrated chains and 2D lattices, running on Quantinuum Helios-1 up to 98 qubits at two-qubit depth at most 42.

Grade 0.498 · 3.5σ above the day's baseline · matched “Qiskit pulse: programming quantum computers through the cloud with pulses” · Cenk Tüysüz, Simon Deconihout, Enrico Rinaldi, Michele Grossi

Figure

Absolute thermal energy-density error versus native two-qubit gate count (left) and depth (right) for a 50-site frustrated chain (top) and a 7×7 TFIM (bottom), showing PP-VarQITE outperforming MPS compilation routes in circuit depth.

Asks

How can finite-temperature thermal states be prepared within shallow circuit depths on noisy quantum hardware using purely classical parameter determination?

Before

Sequential matrix-product-state compilation, which incurs an order-of-magnitude larger gate count and circuit depth to match accuracy.

But

Suffers from an imaginary-time variational delay at intermediate temperatures in frustrated and 2D systems; classical parameter generation requires truncating retained Pauli terms above coefficient threshold cmin⁡.

Tools

Pauli propagation · variational quantum imaginary-time evolution (VarQITE) · thermal purification · Quantinuum Helios-1 trapped-ion processor · Bell-frame recompilation

Abstract

Preparing thermal states on noisy quantum hardware requires circuits that remain shallow at low temperatures. Even when accurate classical state representations are available, compiling them into suitable circuits can be costly. We introduce PP-VarQITE, combining Pauli propagation with variational quantum imaginary-time evolution to determine circuit parameters entirely classically, with target temperatures encoded in the angles of a fixed circuit architecture. In numerical studies of Ising and frustrated Heisenberg models, we recover low-temperature energies and correlations using up to 100 qubits. Across the frustrated chain and two-dimensional lattice, our circuits are approximately two to ten times shallower than the lowest-depth circuits from sequential tensor-network compilation. These shallow circuits enable us to prepare a 48-site frustrated chain and a 7×7 Ising lattice using 96 and 98 qubits on the Quantinuum Helios trapped-ion quantum processor. We reproduce the development of dimer order and lattice-wide correlations from high to low temperatures, with the lattice circuits requiring at most 42 two-qubit layers. Through classical circuit design, we demonstrate low-temperature state preparation at circuit sizes beyond the practical reach of statevector simulation.

item.title: Binary-Tree Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm for the Maximum k-Cut Problem
item.description:
Skim new method — BT-QAOA decomposes Max-k-Cut into at most 2k−3 standard MaxCut QAOA instances, reducing native CZ gate counts from 10855.2 (k=3) and 9748.8 (k=4) under binary encoding to 1866.4 on 24-vertex random graphs while raising the estimated circuit success probability by over 27 orders of magnitude.

Grade 0.431 · 2.7σ above the day's baseline · matched “Tackling the Qubit Mapping Problem for NISQ-Era Quantum Devices”

Figure

Compiled native CZ gate counts (left) and estimated circuit success probability (right) plotted against vertex count n for Kn and G(n,1/2) graphs under IBM Torino calibrations.

Asks

Can multiway graph partitioning (Max-k-Cut) be solved via QAOA without direct multistate encodings that inflate qubit counts or circuit depths?

Before

Binary encoding required n⌈log2⁡k⌉ qubits and multiqubit Pauli decompositions (6 to 8 CNOTs per edge per layer for k=3,4), yielding an ESP of roughly 10−32 on 24-vertex random graphs at p=2.

But

Evaluated via noiseless statevector simulations on up to 24-vertex graphs and hardware compilation without experimental execution on the processor.

Tools

Binary-tree recursive partitioning · Standard MaxCut QAOA (p=2) · Qiskit transpilation on IBM Torino architecture

Abstract

The maximum k-cut (Max-k-Cut) problem, as a natural generalization of the maximum-cut (MaxCut) problem, has broader applications in practical engineering. To solve this problem on quantum devices, existing studies typically encode the k possible subset assignments of each vertex within the quantum approximate optimization algorithm (QAOA), which directly causes the required quantum resources to grow substantially with k. Here we propose a binary-tree quantum approximate optimization algorithm (BT-QAOA), which solves the Max-k-Cut problem by applying standard MaxCut QAOA to at most 2k-3 subproblems. Specifically, after solving MaxCut once on the full vertex set, each subsequent step splits only the subset that yields the largest cut-value gain. This process is equivalent to constructing a binary tree whose leaf nodes after k-1 steps form an approximate solution to the Max-k-Cut problem. Furthermore, we derive a theoretical lower bound on the approximation ratio in terms of the single-step splitting quality, showing that the overall approximation ratio does not decay exponentially across multiple splits. Numerical simulations show that BT-QAOA substantially reduces the single-circuit qubit and gate overhead while maintaining a high approximation ratio, improving the estimated success probability of a single compiled circuit by orders of magnitude. This work effectively expands the practical reach of QAOA on near-term quantum hardware, offering a new route for solving more complex real-world optimization problems with limited quantum resources.
